growth_story.headline: Coups and the 2013 civil war have left income per person below its 1960 level, and a gold-led spurt in 2025 has done little for most households.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in the Central African Republic peaked in 1978. It is now 34.7 percent below that peak and lower than in 1960. Growth averaged -1.9 percent a year in 1990–2000, a decade in which elections did not end coups and violent changes of power, and the World Bank says income per person kept shrinking into the mid-2000s. The 2001–2009 era averaged 1.4 percent a year, with the World Bank dating a burst of faster growth to the years just before the 2013 crisis. The 2013 civil war cut income per person by 36.8 percent in one year, so 2010–2017 averaged -1.8 percent even though recovery began in 2015. Since 2018 growth has averaged 0.2 percent a year, as the pandemic, a political crisis after the December 2020 elections, erratic fuel supply and shrinking aid held activity back.

threads.title: A history of coups
threads.text: Power has changed hands by force again and again since independence, and successive coups brought economic crises. The World Bank says income per person kept falling from the late 1990s into the mid-2000s, through a coup in 2003.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank describes 2025 as an exceptional gold-driven expansion, but in the data income per person rose only 1.0 percent that year. Fast population growth takes up much of the gain. The World Bank also says its 2025 figure rests partly on better recording of gold output and newly rebased national accounts, which the data series here may not yet reflect.
